rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes '256' to '257' ONLY in the comment text on line 18: '// Use 256 threads per block'. The actual constant definition 'const int threads = 256;' on line 19 is UNCHANGED. Comments are stripped during compilation, so both versions compile to identical CUDA kernels. The kernel launch uses threads=256 (from host code line 67), and the kernel-local constant threads=256 (line 19) is also unchanged.
rounds.survival_reason: This mutant is truly semantically equivalent. The mutation testing tool detected a change in the source text, but the change occurs within a C++ comment ('// Use 256 threads...' → '// Use 257 threads...'). Comments are completely ignored by the CUDA compiler and have zero effect on the generated binary code. The actual constant `const int threads = 256;` that controls the kernel's behavior remains unchanged. Both the original and mutated versions compile to bit-identical CUDA kernels, which is why all 112 rounds of bitwise comparison and 138 rounds of deterministic testing show identical outputs. No value-level test can distinguish between two programs with identical compiled code.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable - the mutation is in a C++ comment which has no effect on compiled code. The actual numeric constant 'threads = 256' used in kernel execution is unchanged. Both versions produce identical CUDA binaries.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should exclude comments from the mutation scope, or use AST-based mutation that only targets actual code nodes rather than text patterns. Alternatively, implement a 'compiled binary equivalence' check that detects when mutations don't affect the generated machine code, avoiding wasted testing resources on semantically-identical mutants.
